title: Oxidative stress biology & antioxidant supplements
summary: Reactive oxygen species are normal signalling molecules at low levels (oxidative eustress) and damaging only in excess (distress). Defence is dominated by enzymes such as peroxiredoxins, glutathione peroxidases and the Nrf2-controlled glutathione system, not by dietary scavengers. Large RCTs show high-dose antioxidant supplements (beta-carotene, vitamin E, cocktails) do not prevent disease and some cause harm. Plant compounds most likely help through mild Nrf2/hormetic signalling and gut effects, and ORAC-type 'antioxidant capacity' numbers are meaningless for health.

factors.name: Vitamin C supplements (ascorbic acid)
factors.headline: No effect on cardiovascular disease, cancer or mortality in large RCTs. Shortens colds by about 8% and halves cold risk only under extreme physical stress. About 1 g/day doubles kidney-stone risk in men.

dose.effective: Body stores saturate with diet alone: cells saturate at ~100 mg/day and plasma at ~1,000 mg/day. 1-2 servings of fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C cover the steep part of the curve (30-100 mg).
dose.studied_range: 120 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX) to 500 mg/day (PHS II) for outcomes; 200 mg to 2 g/day for colds
dose.too_much: ≥1,000 mg/day: about twice the kidney-stone risk in men (RR 1.95); 1 g/day blunted endurance-training adaptations.
dose.timeframe: Outcome trials ran for ~8 years with no effect
dose.notes: Oral absorption is tightly controlled (1.25 g oral peak ~135 µmol/L vs ~885 µmol/L IV), so megadoses mostly end up in urine. Pharmacological levels need IV dosing.

factors.mechanism: Water-soluble electron donor that regenerates vitamin E and is a cofactor for many enzymes. A true antioxidant at physiological levels, but once someone is replete, extra intake does not raise tissue levels and cannot compete with peroxiredoxins and GPx for H2O2. Large doses can blunt ROS-dependent training signals (PGC-1α, mitochondrial biogenesis).
factors.interactions: Taken around training it can cancel adaptive signalling, the same issue as [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Combined with vitamin E it showed no benefit in PHS II. Correcting deficiency is useful; adding more on top of a vegetable-rich diet adds nothing measurable.
factors.caveats: The 'megadose vitamin C' claims come from oral pharmacokinetics that cannot reach the plasma levels seen with IV dosing. Cold prevention works only for marathon runners, skiers and soldiers in subarctic conditions. Kidney-stone risk is relevant for men and people prone to stones.

factors.name: Vitamin E supplements (alpha-tocopherol)
factors.headline: No cardiovascular or cancer benefit in more than 100,000 trial participants. 400 IU/day raised prostate cancer by 17%, hemorrhagic stroke by 22-74% and heart failure by 13%, and high doses slightly raise mortality.

dose.effective: No supplemental dose has shown an outcome benefit; get vitamin E from food (nuts, seeds, plant oils).
dose.studied_range: 50 mg/day (ATBC) to 400 IU/day (HOPE, SELECT) or 600 IU every other day (WHS); 200-3,200 IU in biomarker studies
dose.too_much: ≥400 IU/day: +39 deaths per 10,000 (meta-analysis); risk rises above ~150 IU/day. Prostate cancer HR 1.17 at 400 IU/day (SELECT).
dose.timeframe: Lowering F2-isoprostanes needed ≥1,600 IU/day for 16 weeks; outcome trials ran 4.5-10 years
dose.notes: Doses used in outcome trials (400 IU) were too low to change oxidative-stress markers but high enough for bleeding effects. USPSTF grade D (recommends against).

factors.mechanism: Lipid-soluble chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes and LDL. In replete people extra intake does not lower lipid peroxidation at practical doses. The pattern of more hemorrhagic and fewer ischemic strokes is consistent with an antithrombotic effect, though the exact mechanism was not established in these trials.
factors.interactions: Effect on prostate cancer depended on selenium status (risk raised in low-selenium men) [selenium-supplement]. Combined with vitamin C it blunted exercise-induced insulin-sensitivity gains [vitamin-c-supplement]. Combined with NAC it accelerated tumour growth in mice [n-acetylcysteine].
factors.caveats: Observational data (supplement users had less heart disease) were confounded by healthy-user bias, and RCTs reversed the conclusion. WHS showed a 24% reduction in CV death as a secondary outcome, which was not replicated. Hemorrhagic stroke risk matters for people on anticoagulants.

factors.name: Beta-carotene supplements
factors.headline: At 20-30 mg/day, beta-carotene raised lung cancer by 18-28% and total mortality by 8-17% in smokers and asbestos-exposed workers. No benefit for anyone, and USPSTF recommends against it.

dose.effective: None as a supplement. Food carotenoids (carrots, leafy greens, sweet potato) are a different matter.
dose.studied_range: 6 mg/day (SU.VI.MAX mix) to 20-30 mg/day (ATBC, CARET, HPS)
dose.too_much: 20-30 mg/day: lung cancer RR 1.16-1.28, stomach cancer RR 1.34; harm concentrated in smokers and asbestos workers.
dose.timeframe: Excess lung cancer appeared within the 4-8 year trial periods
dose.notes: CARET combined it with 25,000 IU retinol; Cochrane also found dose-related mortality with vitamin A. Smokers should avoid all beta-carotene and vitamin A supplements.

factors.mechanism: At pharmacological doses in a smoke-oxidised lung, beta-carotene lowers lung retinoic acid and RARβ signalling, and raises AP-1/cyclin D1 proliferation signals. In ferrets, a ~30 mg/day-equivalent dose caused squamous metaplasia and a ~6 mg/day-equivalent dose did not. This is a clear example of dose- and context-dependent pro-oxidant harm.
factors.interactions: The harm is amplified by [tobacco-smoking] and asbestos exposure. Part of [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail] and HPS regimens.
factors.caveats: Observational studies linked high blood beta-carotene to lower cancer risk, probably because it marks high fruit and vegetable intake. Supplements reversed this. Multivitamins with small amounts (a few mg) have not shown this harm.

factors.name: Selenium supplements
factors.headline: No cancer prevention (Cochrane RR 1.01). In people who already have adequate selenium, 200 µg/day may raise type 2 diabetes risk (HR 1.55) and high-grade prostate cancer (+91%). Benefit is plausible only if status is low.

dose.effective: Only correct a documented deficiency or very low intake. Most people in North America get enough from food.
dose.studied_range: 100 µg/day (SU.VI.MAX) to 200 µg/day selenomethionine or selenised yeast (SELECT, NPC)
dose.too_much: 200 µg/day in replete people: diabetes HR 1.55 (2.70 in top baseline tertile); high-grade prostate cancer +91% if baseline selenium is high.
dose.timeframe: Diabetes signal over ~7.7 years; prostate cancer over 5-7 years

factors.mechanism: Selenium is the active-site element of glutathione peroxidases and thioredoxin reductases, so deficiency impairs peroxide removal. Above repletion there is no further gain, and the reason for the diabetes signal in replete people is not established.
factors.interactions: Interacts with vitamin E status in prostate cancer risk [vitamin-e-supplement]. Selenium co-treatment enhanced sulforaphane's cytoprotection in vitro, but this has not been studied in humans.
factors.caveats: Cancer results from trials have been mixed, and SELECT and the Cochrane review found no benefit. Many 'antioxidant' blends include 50-200 µg selenium, which adds to dietary intake.

factors.name: Standard multivitamin/mineral (nutritional doses)
factors.headline: A daily standard multivitamin cut total cancer by about 8% in older men (PHS II), with no cardiovascular effect. USPSTF rates the evidence insufficient. It works as nutrient insurance, not as an antioxidant.

dose.effective: One standard multivitamin/mineral daily with nutrients near RDA levels (not 'mega' or 'antioxidant formula').
dose.studied_range: RDA-level combinations; SU.VI.MAX: vitamin C 120 mg, E 30 mg, beta-carotene 6 mg, Se 100 µg, Zn 20 mg
dose.too_much: Avoid formulas with high-dose beta-carotene or vitamin A (especially smokers), vitamin E ≥400 IU, or selenium ≥200 µg.
dose.timeframe: Cancer effect seen after ~11 years in PHS II; 7.5 years in SU.VI.MAX
dose.notes: Benefit is most plausible in people with poor diets or low baseline status (SU.VI.MAX: effect in men, who had lower baseline beta-carotene).

factors.mechanism: Probably corrects marginal micronutrient shortfalls, including selenium, zinc and B vitamins that support endogenous antioxidant enzymes and DNA synthesis and repair, rather than any scavenging effect.
factors.interactions: Do not confuse with [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail]. Adds to dietary selenium and vitamin A [selenium-supplement] [beta-carotene-supplement].
factors.caveats: Evidence comes mostly from male physicians and French adults; the results may not transfer to women or well-nourished groups. The effect size is small and USPSTF calls the evidence insufficient.

factors.name: High-dose 'antioxidant formula' supplements (vitamin C + E + beta-carotene/A, etc.)
factors.headline: Pooled over 78 RCTs, antioxidant supplements did not lower mortality and slightly raised it in low-bias trials (RR 1.04). A 20,536-person trial of vitamin E + C + beta-carotene found no effect at all. Around exercise they block training benefits.

dose.studied_range: e.g. vitamin E 600 mg + C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg/day (HPS); vitamin C 1,000 mg + E 400 IU/day (exercise studies)
dose.too_much: Any dose at these levels: no benefit; beta-carotene, vitamin A and vitamin E components carry the documented harms.
dose.timeframe: Exercise-blunting effect within 4 weeks; mortality signal over years
dose.notes: Raising blood vitamin levels does not mean oxidative damage was reduced; HPS raised levels 'substantially' with zero outcome change.

factors.mechanism: Suppresses ROS signals needed for adaptation (insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis, endogenous antioxidant enzyme induction). In tumours, lowering ROS can release p53-dependent brakes and increase metastasis (mouse data). Endogenous enzymatic defences do not respond to extra dietary antioxidants once someone is replete.
factors.interactions: Antagonises the adaptive (hormetic) benefits of exercise. Contains [vitamin-e-supplement] and [beta-carotene-supplement] harms. Redundant with endogenous defences.
factors.caveats: Marketing often cites ORAC or 'total antioxidant capacity' values, which USDA abandoned in 2012 because they have no demonstrated in-vivo relevance.

factors.name: N-acetylcysteine (NAC)
factors.headline: NAC raises glutathione and improved performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunts muscle repair signalling. In mouse cancer models it accelerated tumour growth and metastasis.

dose.effective: 1,200 mg/day (600 mg twice daily) for 30 days in people with low baseline glutathione
dose.studied_range: 1,200 mg/day for 30 days (performance trial); short courses in exercise-recovery studies
dose.too_much: No defined toxicity threshold at these doses, but caution in people with active or past cancer (mouse data) and around training (blunted adaptation).
dose.timeframe: Glutathione restored within 30 days in deficient individuals
dose.notes: Benefit depends on baseline redox status; there is no routine clinical test, and this is a research approach.

factors.mechanism: Supplies cysteine, the limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis via glutamate-cysteine ligase. By raising GSH it can blunt redox-sensitive signalling (Akt/mTOR, NF-kB) needed for repair, and in tumour cells it can increase glutathione-dependent migration.
factors.interactions: Combined with glycine as [glynac]. Redundant with a high-protein diet rich in sulfur amino acids, and with Nrf2 activators that induce GCL. Antagonises exercise adaptation like [high-dose-antioxidant-cocktail].
factors.caveats: Popular as a 'master antioxidant' supplement. Human outcome data in healthy people are lacking, and the tumour-promotion findings come from mice with existing tumours.

factors.name: Glycine + N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC)
factors.headline: In older adults with low glutathione, glycine plus NAC restored glutathione, lowered F2-isoprostanes and in a 24-person RCT improved mitochondrial, metabolic and physical-function measures. The trials are small and mostly from one group.

dose.effective: Glycine 1.33 mmol/kg/day + cysteine 0.81 mmol/kg/day as NAC (roughly 100 mg/kg glycine + 130 mg/kg NAC; ~7 g + ~9 g/day at 70 kg)
dose.studied_range: Same weight-based dose for 2 weeks to 24 weeks
dose.too_much: Long-term safety beyond 24 weeks not established; same cancer caveat as NAC.
dose.timeframe: Changes reported at 16-24 weeks; benefits declined within 12 weeks of stopping
dose.notes: Relevant mainly to older adults; young adults already have normal glutathione synthesis.

factors.mechanism: Supplies both limiting precursors (cysteine and glycine) for glutathione synthesis, which is reduced with aging. This restores GSH concentration and synthesis rate and lowers oxidative damage.
factors.interactions: Overlaps with [n-acetylcysteine]. Probably redundant in people with high protein intake and normal glutathione.
factors.caveats: Evidence comes from small open-label and placebo-controlled trials from a single research group, with no hard outcomes. The large doses are not those in typical over-the-counter products.

factors.name: Mitochondria-targeted antioxidant (MitoQ)
factors.headline: 20 mg/day MitoQ for 6 weeks improved flow-mediated dilation by 42% in 20 older adults with impaired endothelial function. This is a single small crossover trial without outcome data.

dose.notes: Proprietary compound; independent replication is limited.

factors.mechanism: A ubiquinone attached to a lipophilic cation that accumulates in the mitochondrial matrix, aiming to quench mitochondrial ROS where generic antioxidants cannot reach.
factors.interactions: Could in theory blunt mitohormetic signalling from exercise, like other antioxidants. This has not been tested.
factors.caveats: Small, short-term study measuring a surrogate endpoint only.

factors.name: Isolated polyphenol capsules (quercetin, resveratrol, grape-seed, etc.)
factors.headline: Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as metabolites. Effects in human trials are small and mostly on biomarkers, and no outcome benefit is established for capsules.

dose.studied_range: Tens to hundreds of mg/day in short biomarker studies
dose.timeframe: Transient plasma exposure after each dose
dose.notes: Bioavailability varies over 100-fold by compound (urinary recovery 0.3-43%); isoflavones and gallic acid are best absorbed, proanthocyanidins and anthocyanins worst.

factors.mechanism: Direct scavenging in plasma is implausible at these concentrations. Likely actions are mild electrophilic Nrf2 activation, modulation of NF-kB and endothelial signalling, and local effects in the gut, where much of the dose and its microbial metabolites act.
factors.interactions: May act additively with other Nrf2 activators in vitro; human interaction data are lacking. The rise in plasma antioxidant capacity after polyphenol foods is mostly uric acid.
factors.caveats: Cell-culture 'antioxidant' effects are often artefacts of polyphenols oxidising in culture media. Whole foods with the same polyphenols carry fibre and other components.

factors.name: Excess body fat (especially visceral adiposity)
factors.headline: Fat mass tracks systemic oxidative stress. BMI was one of the strongest independent correlates of urinary F2-isoprostanes in 2,828 Framingham participants, through adipose NADPH oxidase and inflammation.

dose.effective: Reducing excess fat mass (see lifestyle area for specifics).
dose.notes: Mechanistic and cross-sectional human evidence. Intervention data are covered by the lifestyle area.

factors.mechanism: In expanded adipose tissue, free fatty acids activate NADPH oxidase and antioxidant enzymes fall, raising ROS. This disrupts adipokines (lower adiponectin, higher IL-6, MCP-1 and PAI-1) and drives systemic low-grade inflammation through NF-kB. Nutrient excess also raises mitochondrial superoxide.
factors.interactions: Compounds [hyperglycemia-glucose-swings] and [chronic-inflammation]. Supplements do not offset it.
factors.caveats: Most human data are associations. The causal chain is supported by mouse NOX-inhibitor experiments.

factors.name: High blood glucose and post-meal glucose spikes
factors.headline: In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2α tracked glucose variability (r = 0.86) and post-meal glucose, not HbA1c. Hyperglycaemia drives mitochondrial superoxide and AGE formation.

dose.effective: Limit post-meal glucose excursions and keep glucose in the normal range (see food and lifestyle areas).
dose.notes: Dietary AGEs from dry-heat cooking add to the endogenous load (10- to 100-fold more than uncooked).

factors.mechanism: Excess glucose makes the mitochondrial ETC overproduce superoxide, which activates the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways. AGEs bind RAGE, activating NOX and NF-kB. Postprandial hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia transiently raise oxidative stress and impair endothelial function.
factors.interactions: Compounds [excess-adiposity]. Antioxidants taken with a meal can attenuate postprandial oxidative stress, but this has not translated into supplement benefits.
factors.caveats: The Monnier study is small (21 patients). The extent to which glucose swings matter in non-diabetic people is less established.

factors.name: Tobacco smoking
factors.headline: Smoking roughly doubles plasma F2-isoprostanes, which fall measurably within 2 weeks of quitting. It raises urinary 8-OHdG and turns beta-carotene supplements harmful.

dose.timeframe: F2-isoprostanes fell significantly after 2 weeks of abstinence
dose.notes: Smokers should avoid beta-carotene and high-dose vitamin A supplements.

factors.mechanism: Cigarette smoke delivers large amounts of radicals and oxidants directly and recruits activated inflammatory cells to the lung. Tumours with activating NRF2 mutations are enriched in smokers.
factors.interactions: Strongly interacts with [beta-carotene-supplement] (lung cancer RR 1.18-1.28). NRF2-mutant tumours occur especially in smokers.

factors.name: Chronic low-grade inflammation
factors.headline: Activated neutrophils and macrophages are a major regulated source of oxidants, and ROS and NF-kB amplify each other, so persistent inflammation keeps oxidative stress high.

dose.effective: Treat the source (adiposity, smoking, infection, autoimmune or periodontal disease).
dose.notes: Antioxidant supplements have not reduced inflammatory cardiovascular outcomes in large trials.

factors.mechanism: NOX2 and myeloperoxidase in phagocytes generate superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid that damage endothelium and tissue. ROS modulate NF-kB activation, and NF-kB targets regulate ROS production.
factors.interactions: Fed by [excess-adiposity], [tobacco-smoking] and [hyperglycemia-glucose-swings]. Nrf2 activation can counter NF-kB-driven inflammation.
factors.caveats: Inflammation is also protective acutely. The target is chronic, unresolved inflammation.

mechanisms.name: Redox signalling: oxidative eustress vs distress
mechanisms.description: Reactive oxygen species are not only damaging by-products. Hydrogen peroxide and superoxide are made on purpose by more than 40 enzymes, including NADPH oxidases and the mitochondrial electron transport chain, under the control of growth factors and cytokines. At low nanomolar concentrations, H2O2 acts as a second messenger. It reversibly oxidises specific cysteine thiols on phosphatases, kinases and transcription factors, changing what they do. Sies calls this physiological range (about 1-10 nM H2O2 inside cells) 'oxidative eustress'. Higher concentrations switch on adaptive programmes through master regulators such as Nrf2/KEAP1 and NF-kB. Above about 100 nM, oxidation of lipids, proteins and DNA becomes significant ('oxidative distress'). Peroxiredoxins sit at the centre of this system. They are very abundant peroxidases and also act as sensors: they can be switched off locally so that H2O2 builds up and carries a signal, and they can pass the oxidising equivalent to target proteins that react poorly with H2O2 on their own. The practical consequence is that oxidants are part of normal regulation, and indiscriminate antioxidant loading can block useful signals. Large doses of vitamins C and E, or NAC, blunted the gains in insulin sensitivity, mitochondrial biogenesis and muscle repair signalling that normally follow exercise. This is the main conceptual reason why 'more antioxidants' is not automatically better. It also reframes the goal: keep oxidant production within its signalling range, by avoiding chronic overload such as smoking, nutrient excess and inflammation, rather than trying to remove oxidants altogether.

mechanisms.name: Nrf2 / KEAP1 pathway
mechanisms.description: Nrf2 (gene NFE2L2) is the master transcription factor for inducible cytoprotection. Its targets include NQO1, heme oxygenase-1, the glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits that limit glutathione synthesis, glutathione S-transferases, thioredoxin reductase, and enzymes that regenerate NADPH. Under resting conditions KEAP1 binds Nrf2 and acts as an adaptor for a Cul3 ubiquitin ligase, so Nrf2 is degraded with a half-life under 20 minutes. KEAP1 has reactive cysteines that act as sensors. Electrophiles such as sulforaphane and other isothiocyanates, Michael acceptors such as curcumin, oxidised lipids and H2O2 modify these cysteines and stop Nrf2 from being degraded. Nrf2 then accumulates in the nucleus and drives genes with antioxidant response elements. Because activation works by de-repression, it is fast and transient: when the activator is cleared, Nrf2 is degraded again within minutes. These 'indirect antioxidants' act through long-lived catalytic enzymes. Unlike direct scavengers, they are not consumed and are unlikely to act as pro-oxidants. In humans, sulforaphane from broccoli sprouts raises phase II enzyme expression in airway cells in a dose-dependent way. A full-strength sprout beverage increased benzene detoxification by 63%, while half and one-fifth doses did not. The effect persisted over 12 weeks without tolerance. Exercise and caloric restriction also activate Nrf2. Responses are modest and self-limiting by design. Chronic maximal activation is harmful: Keap1-null mice die soon after birth, cancers carry activating NRF2/KEAP1 mutations that confer chemoresistance, oncogenes raise Nrf2 to support tumours, and the potent drug activator bardoxolone methyl increased heart failure in kidney patients. The dietary goal is therefore intermittent, moderate activation, not maximal activation.

mechanisms.name: Direct radical scavenging by dietary antioxidants
mechanisms.description: The classic idea is that vitamin C, vitamin E, carotenoids and polyphenols protect us by reacting with free radicals before those radicals reach lipids, proteins or DNA. This chemistry is real in the test tube, but in the body it is limited by kinetics, concentration and location. Peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases remove H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides so quickly, and are present in such amounts, that small-molecule antioxidants cannot capture a meaningful share of peroxide inside cells. Forman, Davies and Ursini conclude that in vivo radical scavenging is kinetically ineffective as a defence, and that enzymatic two-electron reduction of hydroperoxides is the real mechanism. Sies states that the main role in antioxidant defence is played by enzymes, not small molecules. Vitamin E as the chain-breaking antioxidant in membranes, and vitamin C, are genuine exceptions, but their effect plateaus once deficiency is corrected. Oral vitamin C is tightly controlled: plasma is saturated at about 1 g/day, and cells at about 100 mg/day. Vitamin E reduced F2-isoprostanes only at 1,600-3,200 IU/day, far above trial doses. Polyphenols reach only about 0-4 µmol/L in plasma, mostly as conjugated metabolites. That is negligible next to urate and ascorbate, and the rise in plasma 'antioxidant capacity' after eating flavonoid-rich food is explained by uric acid. Food ORAC values therefore do not predict in vivo effects, and USDA withdrew its ORAC database in 2012. Direct scavenging may still matter locally in the gut lumen, where polyphenol concentrations are much higher. Elsewhere, the benefits of plant foods are better explained by signalling (Nrf2, NF-kB) and by the microbiome.

mechanisms.name: Mitochondrial ROS (electron transport chain leak)
mechanisms.description: Mitochondria are a major source of superoxide inside cells. Electrons leak from the electron transport chain, mainly at complex I and also at complex III, and reduce oxygen to superoxide in the matrix. SOD2 then converts it to H2O2. Murphy showed that the leak depends on conditions. Superoxide production is high when mitochondria are not making ATP, so the protonmotive force is high and the coenzyme Q pool is reduced, and when the matrix NADH/NAD+ ratio is high. Both situations arise with nutrient excess and physical inactivity. When mitochondria are actively making ATP, production is much lower. For that reason the old textbook figure of '1-2% of oxygen becoming superoxide', based on isolated mitochondria, cannot be applied to living tissue. Mitochondrial ROS have two roles. They signal from mitochondria to the nucleus and drive adaptations such as mitochondrial biogenesis after exercise, a concept called mitohormesis, and antioxidant supplements can block these adaptations. In chronic hyperglycaemia, Brownlee proposed that mitochondrial superoxide overproduction is the single upstream event behind the polyol, AGE, PKC and hexosamine pathways of diabetic vascular damage. Plasma antioxidants cannot easily reach the mitochondrial matrix. That led to mitochondria-targeted compounds such as MitoQ, which improved endothelial function by 42% in a small six-week trial in older adults. The most reliable ways to keep mitochondrial ROS in the signalling range are lifestyle measures that keep mitochondria working and lower nutrient overload: regular activity, avoiding chronic energy excess, and good glucose control.

mechanisms.name: NADPH oxidases and other enzymatic ROS sources (xanthine oxidase, NOS/peroxynitrite)
mechanisms.description: NADPH oxidases (NOX1-5 and DUOX1/2) are the only enzyme family whose main job is to make ROS. NOX2 in neutrophils and macrophages produces the 'respiratory burst' that kills microbes. Other isoforms produce superoxide or H2O2 for signalling in blood vessels, fibroblasts and many other cells. DUOX enzymes supply H2O2 for thyroid hormone synthesis. Excess NOX activity is a recurring theme in chronic disease. In obesity, adipose tissue upregulates NADPH oxidase and downregulates antioxidant enzymes. This raises local and systemic oxidative stress and disrupts adipokines (lower adiponectin, higher IL-6, MCP-1 and PAI-1). A NOX inhibitor reversed these changes and improved diabetes and fatty liver in obese mice. Xanthine oxidase, which converts hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, also makes superoxide and H2O2. It contributes to ischemia-reperfusion injury and is the target of allopurinol and febuxostat. Nitric oxide synthase normally makes protective •NO. When •NO meets superoxide it forms peroxynitrite, a strong oxidant and nitrating agent, and superoxide therefore lowers •NO availability. This is a key mechanism of endothelial dysfunction. Because these enzymes are regulated sources, the most effective interventions target the triggers: excess fat mass, inflammation, hyperglycaemia and smoking. Giving scavengers after the oxidants have been made is less effective. Specific NOX inhibitors are still mostly experimental.

mechanisms.name: Iron, Fenton chemistry and ferroptosis
mechanisms.description: Ferrous iron (and copper) react with hydrogen peroxide in the Fenton reaction. This produces the hydroxyl radical or highly reactive iron-oxo species that oxidise almost any nearby molecule. Since H2O2 is always present at low levels, the body controls oxidative damage largely by keeping iron tightly bound to transferrin, ferritin and heme proteins and limiting the 'labile' iron pool. Free or poorly chelated iron at sites of injury and inflammation greatly increases damage. Iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation drives ferroptosis, a regulated, non-apoptotic form of cell death. In ferroptosis, lipid hydroperoxides build up when glutathione-dependent defences fail, and the process is blocked by iron chelators and lipophilic radical-trapping agents such as ferrostatin-1. Ferroptosis links three mechanisms on this page: the glutathione system, lipid peroxidation, and iron status. It is relevant to neurodegeneration, ischemic injury and cancer therapy. Vitamin C can reduce ferric to ferrous iron in vitro. This is one reason pro-oxidant effects of high-dose antioxidants are discussed, though their importance in vivo at oral doses is unclear because oral vitamin C plasma levels are tightly capped. For the website, the practical messages are to avoid iron supplements unless iron deficiency is documented, and to recognise that iron overload conditions are a genuine source of oxidative stress. Dietary measures that control labile iron in healthy people have not been shown to change outcomes.

mechanisms.name: Lipid peroxidation
mechanisms.description: Lipid peroxidation is a free-radical chain reaction in polyunsaturated fatty acids, most often in membranes and lipoproteins. An initiating radical removes a hydrogen atom next to a double bond. The lipid radical picks up oxygen to become a peroxyl radical, which attacks the next fatty acid, and so on. The chain is broken mainly by vitamin E in membranes, and the resulting hydroperoxides are reduced by glutathione peroxidases. The products are both damage and signals. F2-isoprostanes form non-enzymatically from arachidonic acid. When measured by mass spectrometry they are the best-validated in vivo marker of oxidative stress in humans: they rose consistently in the NIH BOSS validation study, are about twice as high in smokers, fall within two weeks of quitting, and track BMI and glucose in the Framingham cohort. Reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal form adducts with proteins and DNA and act as signalling molecules at low levels. Measuring MDA with the TBARS assay is unreliable because it is non-specific and prone to artefacts. Oxidised phospholipids on LDL are associated with angiographic coronary disease. Uncontrolled, iron-catalysed lipid peroxidation executes ferroptosis. Supplements show the gap between mechanism and practice: vitamin E 200-2,000 IU/day did not lower isoprostanes in healthy people, and 1,600 IU/day or more was needed in people with high cholesterol. Lifestyle factors that raise lipid peroxidation (smoking, adiposity, hyperglycaemia) are therefore better targets than chain-breaking supplements.

mechanisms.name: Oxidative DNA damage and repair
mechanisms.description: Hydroxyl radicals and other strong oxidants damage DNA bases and sugars. The best-studied lesion is 8-oxo-7,8-dihydroguanine (8-oxoGua; as the nucleoside, 8-oxo-dG or 8-OHdG). If it is not repaired it can pair with adenine and cause G-to-T transversions, a mutation pattern seen in some cancers. Cells remove such lesions mainly by base-excision repair (OGG1 for 8-oxoGua, plus MUTYH and MTH1 to prevent misincorporation), and the excised products are excreted in urine. Measurement is the main problem. The European Standards Committee on Oxidative DNA Damage (ESCODD) found large disagreements between laboratories, because guanine oxidises artefactually during DNA extraction and processing. The true background in human cells is probably about 0.3-4.2 lesions per million guanines, much lower than early chromatographic estimates. Urinary 8-OHdG measured by chemical methods such as LC-MS/MS is more robust. A meta-analysis of 84 studies put the healthy-adult background at about 3.9 ng/mg creatinine and found higher levels in smokers. In the NIH BOSS study, urinary 8-OHdG rose with a known oxidant insult in most conditions, while DNA strand breaks did not. Cooke and colleagues note that many contradictory disease associations reflect biomarker shortcomings. In practice, urinary 8-oxo-dG by mass spectrometry is a reasonable research marker of whole-body oxidative DNA damage, but ELISA-based values and single-time-point results should be read cautiously. No antioxidant supplement has been shown to lower cancer risk by lowering this marker.

mechanisms.name: Glutathione system and endogenous antioxidant enzymes
mechanisms.description: The enzymatic network does almost all of the body's antioxidant work. Superoxide dismutases (SOD1 in the cytosol, SOD2 in mitochondria, SOD3 outside cells) convert superoxide to H2O2. Catalase, the selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidases and the six peroxiredoxins reduce H2O2 and lipid hydroperoxides to water and alcohols. Glutathione reductase and the thioredoxin/thioredoxin reductase system regenerate these enzymes using NADPH. Glutathione (GSH), a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine, is the most abundant non-protein thiol, at millimolar concentrations inside cells. Its synthesis is limited by cysteine supply and by glutamate-cysteine ligase, which is itself an Nrf2 target. This is why Nrf2 activators raise glutathione and why cysteine donors such as NAC can raise it in people who are short of it. In older adults, red-cell glutathione and its synthesis rate were about half those of young adults, and F2-isoprostanes were higher. Glycine plus NAC restored these values, and a small 16-week RCT reported metabolic and functional improvements. NAC at 1,200 mg/day improved exercise performance and oxidative markers only in people with low baseline glutathione. In replete people it blunted training signals, and in mouse tumour models it accelerated cancer progression and metastasis by raising tumour glutathione. Measuring the GSH/GSSG ratio needs immediate thiol trapping with N-ethylmaleimide, because GSSG is otherwise greatly overestimated. Selenium status matters for GPx activity, but in replete people extra selenium brings no benefit and may raise diabetes risk.

mechanisms.name: Hyperglycaemia, glycation and advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)
mechanisms.description: High glucose drives oxidative stress through several linked routes. Brownlee proposed a unifying mechanism: hyperglycaemia makes the mitochondrial electron transport chain overproduce superoxide, which partly inhibits GAPDH and diverts glycolytic intermediates into four damaging pathways. These are polyol flux, formation of advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), protein kinase C activation, and hexosamine flux. AGEs form when reducing sugars and reactive dicarbonyls such as methylglyoxal modify proteins and lipids. They crosslink matrix proteins and, by binding the receptor RAGE, trigger NOX activation and NF-kB-driven inflammation, which creates more oxidants. Glucose swings may matter more than average glucose. In type 2 diabetes, urinary 8-iso-PGF2alpha correlated strongly with glycaemic variability (MAGE, r = 0.86) and with the postprandial glucose area, but not with HbA1c. 'Postprandial oxidative stress' after high-glucose and high-fat meals is a recognised phenomenon, and a large part of the day is spent in the postprandial state. AGEs also come from the diet. Dry-heat cooking such as grilling, roasting and frying raises the AGE content of foods 10- to 100-fold compared with the uncooked state, while moist-heat methods such as boiling, stewing and steaming generate far less. Practical measures follow from the mechanism: reduce glucose spikes through meal composition, fibre and post-meal activity, and favour moist cooking. Another research area covers the food-specific details.

mechanisms.name: Inflammation and NF-kB
mechanisms.description: Inflammation and oxidative stress drive each other. At sites of inflammation, neutrophils and macrophages assemble NOX2 and release myeloperoxidase, producing superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid. These oxidants kill microbes, but they also open endothelial junctions, damage nearby tissue and recruit more inflammatory cells. The transcription factor NF-kB controls many inflammatory genes (cytokines, adhesion molecules, inducible enzymes). ROS can activate or inhibit NF-kB signalling depending on the cell and the context, and NF-kB targets in turn regulate how much ROS a cell produces. This two-way link means chronic low-grade inflammation, for example from visceral adiposity, smoking, periodontal disease or autoimmune disease, keeps oxidant production high. It also helps explain why plant compounds that modulate signalling, such as Nrf2 activators that dampen NF-kB-driven inflammation, may have effects that scavenging cannot explain. Adipose tissue is a clear example: in obesity, fatty acids activate adipocyte NADPH oxidase and the resulting oxidative stress disrupts adipokines, raising IL-6 and MCP-1 and lowering adiponectin, which feeds systemic inflammation. Treating the inflammatory source (weight loss, stopping smoking, treating infection or autoimmune disease) is the effective lever. Broad antioxidant supplements have not reduced inflammatory cardiovascular or cancer outcomes in large trials.

mechanisms.name: Hormesis, mitohormesis and xenohormesis
mechanisms.description: Hormesis describes a two-phase dose response: a low dose of a stressor triggers protective adaptations, while a high dose causes harm. Mild stressors such as heat, exercise, caloric restriction and some phytochemicals extend lifespan or increase stress resistance in many animal models. 'Mitohormesis' applies this idea to mitochondrial ROS. The transient rise in ROS during exercise or energy restriction triggers lasting increases in antioxidant enzymes, mitochondrial biogenesis and insulin sensitivity, and antioxidant supplements can block these responses. In humans, vitamin C plus vitamin E abolished the gain in insulin sensitivity from four weeks of training, and vitamin C alone blunted mitochondrial biogenesis. Calabrese argues that Nrf2 activation is a common mechanism of hormesis and stresses that the maximal response is modest and capped. Sulforaphane shows a biphasic pattern in vitro: low micromolar levels increased cell proliferation and migration, including in cancer cell lines, while higher levels inhibited them. 'Xenohormesis' proposes that animals evolved to sense plant stress molecules such as polyphenols and isothiocyanates as signals to prepare their own defences. This would explain why such compounds act through signalling pathways and not as stoichiometric scavengers. Forman and colleagues call the electrophilic version 'para-hormesis'. The implications for guidance are that occasional, moderate challenges are the goal, that more stimulus is not always better, and that antioxidant megadoses around training can cancel the benefit.

references.finding: Vitamin E 400 IU/d for 4.5 years had no effect on cardiovascular events (RR 1.05).

references.authors: Lonn E, Bosch J, Yusuf S, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term vitamin E supplementation on cardiovascular events and cancer: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Long-term vitamin E 400 IU/d did not prevent cancer or major CV events and increased heart failure (RR 1.13).

references.authors: Sesso HD, Buring JE, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin E 400 IU every other day and vitamin C 500 mg/d for 8 years had no effect on major CV events; vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke (HR 1.74).

references.authors: Gaziano JM, Glynn RJ, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of prostate and total cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Neither vitamin E nor vitamin C reduced prostate or total cancer over 8 years.

references.authors: Heart Protection Study Collaborative Group
references.title: MRC/BHF Heart Protection Study of antioxidant vitamin supplementation in 20,536 high-risk individuals: a randomised placebo-controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin E 600 mg + vitamin C 250 mg + beta-carotene 20 mg daily raised blood levels but had no effect on vascular events, cancer or mortality over 5 years.

references.authors: Lee IM, Cook NR, Gaziano JM, et al.
references.title: Vitamin E in the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease and cancer: the Women's Health Study: a randomized controlled trial
references.finding: Vitamin E 600 IU every other day gave no overall benefit for CV events, cancer or total mortality; CV death was 24% lower (secondary outcome).

references.authors: Bjelakovic G, Nikolova D, Gluud LL, et al.
references.title: Antioxidant supplements for prevention of mortality in healthy participants and patients with various diseases
references.finding: Antioxidant supplements increased mortality in low-bias trials (RR 1.04); beta-carotene (RR 1.05) and vitamin E (RR 1.03) significantly, vitamin C and selenium not.

references.authors: Miller ER 3rd, Pastor-Barriuso R, Dalal D, et al.
references.title: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality
references.finding: High-dose vitamin E (>=400 IU/d) increased all-cause mortality by 39 per 10,000; risk rose above ~150 IU/d.

references.authors: Schürks M, Glynn RJ, Rist PM, et al.
references.title: Effects of vitamin E on stroke subtypes: meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
references.finding: Vitamin E increased hemorrhagic stroke by 22% and reduced ischemic stroke by 10%, with no effect on total stroke.

references.authors: Druesne-Pecollo N, Latino-Martel P, Norat T, et al.
references.title: Beta-carotene supplementation and cancer risk: a systematic review and metaanalysis of randomized controlled trials
references.finding: Beta-carotene had no effect on overall cancer but at 20-30 mg/d increased lung (RR 1.16) and stomach cancer, especially in smokers and asbestos workers.

references.authors: Liu C, Wang XD, Bronson RT, et al.
references.title: Effects of physiological versus pharmacological beta-carotene supplementation on cell proliferation and histopathological changes in the lungs of cigarette smoke-exposed ferrets
references.finding: In smoke-exposed ferrets, pharmacological beta-carotene (~30 mg/d human equivalent) lowered lung retinoic acid and caused squamous metaplasia; a physiological dose (~6 mg/d) did not.

references.authors: Sayin VI, Ibrahim MX, Larsson E, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants accelerate lung cancer progression in mice
references.finding: NAC and vitamin E accelerated lung tumour progression and shortened survival in mice by reducing ROS, DNA damage and p53 expression.

references.authors: Le Gal K, Ibrahim MX, Wiel C, et al.
references.title: Antioxidants can increase melanoma metastasis in mice
references.finding: NAC and Trolox increased lymph node metastasis of melanoma in mice by raising tumour-cell glutathione and RHOA activation.

references.authors: Roberts LJ 2nd, Oates JA, Linton MF, et al.
references.title: The relationship between dose of vitamin E and suppression of oxidative stress in humans
references.finding: Vitamin E lowered plasma F2-isoprostanes significantly only at 1,600 IU/d (-35%) and 3,200 IU/d (-49%), with maximum effect after 16 weeks.

references.authors: Meagher EA, Barry OP, Lawson JA, et al.
references.title: Effects of vitamin E on lipid peroxidation in healthy persons
references.finding: Vitamin E 200-2,000 IU/d for 8 weeks raised vitamin E levels but did not change urinary isoprostanes or 4-HNE.

references.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force, Mangione CM, Barry MJ, et al.
references.title: Vitamin, Mineral, and Multivitamin Supplementation to Prevent Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
references.finding: USPSTF recommends against beta-carotene or vitamin E for preventing CVD or cancer (grade D); evidence is insufficient for multivitamins and other single or paired nutrients.

references.authors: O'Connor EA, Evans CV, Ivlev I, et al.
references.title: Vitamin and Mineral Supplements for the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease and Cancer: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force
references.finding: Multivitamins were associated with slightly lower cancer incidence (OR 0.93); beta-carotene increased lung cancer and CV mortality; vitamin E had no effect.

references.authors: Hercberg S, Galan P, Preziosi P, et al.
references.title: The SU.VI.MAX Study: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of the health effects of antioxidant vitamins and minerals
references.finding: Nutritional-dose antioxidant mix (vitamin C 120 mg, E 30 mg, beta-carotene 6 mg, Se 100 ug, Zn 20 mg) had no overall effect but lowered cancer (RR 0.69) and mortality in men, not women.

references.authors: Sesso HD, Christen WG, Bubes V, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for 11 years did not reduce major cardiovascular events, MI, stroke or CV mortality.

references.authors: Gaziano JM, Sesso HD, Christen WG, et al.
references.title: Multivitamins in the prevention of cancer in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
references.finding: A daily multivitamin for 11 years modestly reduced total cancer (HR 0.92).

references.authors: Levine M, Conry-Cantilena C, Wang Y, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics in healthy volunteers: evidence for a recommended dietary allowance
references.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
references.finding: Vitamin C plasma concentration is sigmoid with dose: steep between 30-100 mg/d, cells saturated at 100 mg/d, plasma completely saturated at 1,000 mg/d.

references.authors: Padayatty SJ, Sun H, Wang Y, et al.
references.title: Vitamin C pharmacokinetics: implications for oral and intravenous use
references.finding: Oral vitamin C produces tightly controlled plasma levels (1.25 g oral peak ~135 umol/L vs ~885 umol/L IV); only IV achieves pharmacological levels.

references.authors: Hemilä H, Chalker E
references.title: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
references.finding: Regular vitamin C (>=200 mg/d) did not reduce cold incidence in the general population (RR 0.97) but halved it under extreme physical stress, and shortened colds by 8% in adults.

references.authors: Thomas LD, Elinder CG, Tiselius HG, et al.
references.title: Ascorbic acid supplements and kidney stone incidence among men: a prospective study
references.finding: Use of ascorbic acid supplements (~1,000 mg tablets) was associated with about double the risk of kidney stones (RR 1.95).

references.authors: Rayman MP
references.title: Selenium and human health
references.finding: Selenium has a U-shaped relation to health: supplementation may help those with low status but may harm (e.g. type 2 diabetes) those with adequate or high status.

references.authors: Stranges S, Marshall JR, Natarajan R, et al.
references.title: Effects of long-term selenium supplementation on the incidence of type 2 diabetes: a randomized trial
references.finding: Selenium 200 ug/d increased type 2 diabetes incidence (HR 1.55), especially in the top tertile of baseline selenium (HR 2.70).

references.authors: Vinceti M, Filippini T, Del Giovane C, et al.
references.title: Selenium for preventing cancer
references.finding: High-certainty evidence that selenium supplementation does not reduce cancer incidence (RR 1.01) or cancer mortality.

references.authors: Paschalis V, Theodorou AA, Margaritelis NV, et al.
references.title: N-acetylcysteine supplementation increases exercise performance and reduces oxidative stress only in individuals with low levels of glutathione
references.finding: NAC 1,200 mg/d for 30 days restored glutathione, reduced F2-isoprostanes and improved VO2max (~14%) only in people with low baseline glutathione.

references.authors: Sekhar RV, Patel SG, Guthikonda AP, et al.
references.title: Deficient synthesis of glutathione underlies oxidative stress in aging and can be corrected by dietary cysteine and glycine supplementation
references.finding: Older adults had lower red-cell glutathione and synthesis and higher F2-isoprostanes; glycine + cysteine supplementation restored these to young-adult values.

references.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Hsu JW, et al.
references.title: Glycine and N-acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) supplementation in older adults improves glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, insulin resistance, endothelial dysfunction, genotoxicity, muscle strength, and cognition: Results of a pilot clinical trial
references.finding: 24 weeks of GlyNAC in older adults corrected glutathione deficiency and oxidative stress and improved several functional measures; benefits declined after stopping.

references.authors: Kumar P, Liu C, Suliburk J, et al.
references.title: Supplementing Glycine and N-Acetylcysteine (GlyNAC) in Older Adults Improves Glutathione Deficiency, Oxidative Stress, Mitochondrial Dysfunction, Inflammation, Physical Function, and Aging Hallmarks: A Randomized Clinical Trial
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.finding: In a placebo-controlled 16-week RCT, GlyNAC improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, insulin resistance and physical function in older adults.

references.authors: Rossman MJ, Santos-Parker JR, Steward CAC, et al.
references.title: Chronic Supplementation With a Mitochondrial Antioxidant (MitoQ) Improves Vascular Function in Healthy Older Adults
references.finding: MitoQ 20 mg/d for 6 weeks improved brachial flow-mediated dilation by 42% versus placebo, linked to reduced mitochondrial ROS suppression of endothelial function.

references.authors: Manach C, Scalbert A, Morand C, et al.
references.title: Polyphenols: food sources and bioavailability
references.finding: Reviews polyphenol food sources, intakes and bioavailability, which depends strongly on chemical structure.

references.authors: Manach C, Williamson G, Morand C, et al.
references.title: Bioavailability and bioefficacy of polyphenols in humans. I. Review of 97 bioavailability studies
references.finding: After 50 mg aglycone equivalents, plasma polyphenol metabolites reach only 0-4 umol/L and urinary excretion is 0.3-43% of dose, varying greatly by compound.

references.authors: Williamson G, Manach C
references.title: Bioavailability and bioefficacy of polyphenols in humans. II. Review of 93 intervention studies
references.finding: Polyphenol effects in humans are measurable but more limited than in vitro, due to lack of validated biomarkers, long-term studies and bioavailability-aware design.

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: Dietary polyphenols: good, bad, or indifferent for your health?
references.finding: Questions whether dietary polyphenols act as antioxidants in vivo and highlights possible gut-level effects and pro-oxidant artefacts.

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: Are polyphenols antioxidants or pro-oxidants? What do we learn from cell culture and in vivo studies?
references.finding: Neither antioxidant nor pro-oxidant effects of polyphenols are established in humans at achievable levels; many cell-culture results are artefacts of polyphenol oxidation in media.

references.authors: Del Rio D, Rodriguez-Mateos A, Spencer JP, et al.
references.title: Dietary (poly)phenolics in human health: structures, bioavailability, and evidence of protective effects against chronic diseases
references.finding: Most dietary (poly)phenolics are extensively metabolised, with large fractions reaching the colon where microbes produce absorbable phenolic catabolites.

references.authors: Halliwell B
references.title: The antioxidant paradox: less paradoxical now?
references.finding: The antioxidant paradox arises because endogenous defences are tightly regulated and body antioxidant status and oxidative damage are largely unresponsive to high-dose dietary antioxidants.

references.authors: Furukawa S, Fujita T, Shimabukuro M, et al.
references.title: Increased oxidative stress in obesity and its impact on metabolic syndrome
references.finding: Fat accumulation correlated with systemic oxidative stress in humans and mice; adipose NADPH oxidase drove ROS and adipokine dysregulation, and NOX inhibition improved metabolic disease in mice.

references.authors: Monnier L, Mas E, Ginet C, et al.
references.title: Activation of oxidative stress by acute glucose fluctuations compared with sustained chronic hyperglycemia in patients with type 2 diabetes
references.finding: Urinary 8-iso-PGF2a correlated strongly with glycaemic variability (MAGE, r=0.86) and postprandial glucose, not with HbA1c.

references.authors: Brownlee M
references.title: Biochemistry and molecular cell biology of diabetic complications
references.finding: Proposes that hyperglycaemia-induced mitochondrial superoxide overproduction underlies the four main pathways of diabetic vascular damage.

references.authors: Sies H, Stahl W, Sevanian A
references.title: Nutritional, dietary and postprandial oxidative stress
references.finding: Defines postprandial oxidative stress from hyperglycaemia and hyperlipidaemia and notes that dietary antioxidants/polyphenols with meals can attenuate it.

references.authors: Uribarri J, Woodruff S, Goodman S, et al.
references.title: Advanced glycation end products in foods and a practical guide to their reduction in the diet
references.finding: Database of dietary AGE content; dry-heat cooking raises AGE content 10- to 100-fold over the uncooked state.

references.authors: Morgan MJ, Liu ZG
references.title: Crosstalk of reactive oxygen species and NF-κB signaling
references.finding: ROS and NF-kB regulate each other: NF-kB targets control ROS levels and ROS can activate or inhibit NF-kB signalling.

references.authors: Mittal M, Siddiqui MR, Tran K, et al.
references.title: Reactive oxygen species in inflammation and tissue injury
references.finding: Neutrophil-derived ROS at inflammatory sites cause endothelial dysfunction and tissue injury.
